items.title: Bacteria count themselves before acting
items.claim: A single Vibrio fischeri bacterium doesn't glow. A dense colony of them lights up the inside of squid light organs and certain Hawaiian fish. The bacteria sense how many bacteria are around them and only switch on bioluminescence when there are enough to matter.
items.prompt: How does a bacterium know how many others are nearby?

options.text: Quorum sensing — each cell secretes a small molecule (an autoinducer); local concentration of autoinducer rises with population density, and at threshold activates gene expression
They wait a fixed time before turning on

items.reveal:
Quorum sensing was discovered in Vibrio fischeri by Hastings and Nealson in the 1970s. Each bacterium continuously produces and secretes a homoserine lactone. At low cell density it diffuses away; at high density it accumulates, enters cells and binds a transcription factor that activates luciferase genes.

Bonnie Bassler's group showed in the 1990s that many bacteria use multiple quorum signals — one species-specific, one universal (AI-2). The universal one allows cross-species 'eavesdropping' on population density of other bacteria.

Pathogens use quorum sensing to time virulence factor expression: stay quiet until there are enough cells to overwhelm the host. Anti-quorum-sensing drugs are an active research area for antibiotic alternatives.
items.why: Bacteria are imagined as solitary cells acting independently. Many of their key behaviours — virulence, biofilm formation, bioluminescence — are coordinated through chemical signalling networks.

items.title: Elephants need hairs to STAY COOL
items.claim: Big animals are well-insulated by sheer size — surface area to volume ratio drops as you scale up. So why do elephants have sparse but persistent hairs, in a hot environment where insulation is the last thing they need?
items.prompt: What's the function of an elephant's hairs?

options.text: They INCREASE convective heat loss — the sparse hairs disrupt the still air layer at the skin surface and allow more efficient cooling than bare skin would

items.reveal_title: Surface area scaling and thermal management
items.reveal:
Animal mass scales as length cubed; surface area as length squared. Doubling an animal's linear size doubles its surface-to-volume ratio's inverse — large animals have proportionally less surface area to dump heat through.

Elephants generate huge metabolic heat (about 2500 watts at rest for a 4 tonne adult) but have proportionally tiny skin. They are constantly battling overheating. Their hairs, ears (huge for their body), wallowing in mud, and behavioural cooling all serve heat dissipation.

Cordeschi and colleagues (2012) modelled elephant hair density and showed sparse hairs improve heat loss by about 5 to 20 percent — likely a real evolutionary purpose.
items.why: Hair is associated with warmth. For animals at the wrong end of the surface-to-volume scaling, hair can do the opposite.

items.title: Every leaf contains the descendants of a captured bacterium
items.claim: Chloroplasts have their own circular DNA, their own ribosomes, a double membrane, and divide by fission. About 1.5 billion years ago, a eukaryotic cell engulfed a cyanobacterium and kept it as a permanent tenant.
items.prompt: What's the strongest single line of evidence?

options.text: Chloroplast 16S ribosomal RNA sequences group phylogenetically with free-living cyanobacteria, not with any eukaryotic structure — they are bacterial by descent
Chloroplasts can be removed without killing the plant

items.reveal:
The original engulfment (primary endosymbiosis) gave rise to the chloroplasts of red algae, green algae and land plants. The cyanobacterial guest lost most of its genome to the host nucleus over time, but retained ~120 genes — mostly for photosynthesis machinery.

Later, secondary endosymbiosis occurred: a non-photosynthetic eukaryote engulfed a red or green alga. The result is the four-membraned plastids of diatoms, brown algae, and apicomplexans (the parasites that cause malaria still carry a vestigial non-photosynthetic plastid).

The apicoplast in Plasmodium is a drug target — anti-bacterial drugs (clindamycin, doxycycline) kill malaria parasites by poisoning their plastid's bacterial-style ribosomes.

Lynn Margulis pushed endosymbiosis from a fringe idea to consensus. Without it, photosynthesis would never have entered eukaryotic life.
items.why: Plant cells feel monolithic. They are chimeras — green parts of every leaf descend from a captured bacterium that never left.
